title: What is application allowlisting?
summary: AI agents that autonomously resolve IT issues on endpoints and in the cloud.
body_text: What is allowlisting? In today’s cybersecurity landscape, blocking malware and untrusted software demands more than reactive antivirus measures. Application allowlisting - where only trusted software is permitted to run - offers a robust “default-deny” security posture. Application allowlisting ensures that only trusted applications can execute on a device. idemeum’s agent intercepts every process launch - if an application lacks an explicit allow rule, execution is denied. This proactive “zero trust for executables” model blocks ransomware, unknown software, and lateral movement. Unlike blocklists that try to catch bad actors, allowlisting denies all by default and grants access only to verified software - drastically reducing the attack surface. Allowlisting vs. Blocklisting Although “application allowlisting” and “application whitelisting” refer to the same thing, application allowlisting is the preferred language for describing this security capability. According to the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre , equating “white” with “good, permitted, and safe” and black with “bad, dangerous, and forbidden” is problematic, especially when another less ambiguous term is available to describe the same activities. It is the same case for “blocklisting” (or denylisting) and “blacklisting.” While using the term “blacklisting” to describe undesirable attributes in cybersecurity was common, the neutral “blocklisting” is now in favor. Using a predefined list of “bad” applications, blocklisting software typically compares any applications attempting to run on the network with the list of blocked applications. If the application is not on the blocklist, it is allowed to proceed. For example, conventional antivirus software uses blocklisting to prevent known malware from being executed on a computer system. Since application allowlisting denies unlisted applications and application blocklisting allows unlisted applications, application allowlisting is arguably more secure than application blocklisting. Which approach aligns with Zero Trust? Application control can take one of two approaches, allowlisting or blocklisting. Although both seek to place some control over the applications in an environment, only allowlisting truly aligns with the Zero Trust "never trust, always verify" philosophy. In other words, nothing can be explicitly trusted, and every person, application, and network connection must be restricted to only the exact access they require. According to CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) #StopRansomware Guide update published in May 2023, "Use allowlisting rather than attempting to list and deny every possible permutation of applications in a network environment." Use cases Use case Description Ransomware defense Block unknown binaries and scripts from executing - even if they’re downloaded by a trusted process. Regulatory compliance Enforce strict control for HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and NIST standards. least privilege access Combine with Endpoint Privilege Management (EPM) to remove admin rights while keeping teams productive. Audit Get full visibility into what’s executed across your fleet - instantly and historically. Idemeum allowlisting Traditional allowlisting approaches are known for being rigid, hard to manage, and generate a lot of operational load for IT / MSP teams. This is where idemeum brings innovation: a simple, intelligent, and scalable solution that makes allowlisting practical for real-world use. Feature Description Default deny with OS trust Idemeum automatically trusts essential Windows system binaries (OSBinary), ensuring no disruption to core operations. At the same time, it blocks signed but dangerous executables like mshta.exe or powershell.exe - often exploited in fileless attacks. Powerful and flexible rule engine Define rules by file path, filename, SHA-256 hash, publisher certificate, or regex patterns. Match criteria using certificate metadata like Common Name (CN), Organization (O), and Organizational Unit (OU). One-click catalog rules Idemeum provides a pre-built catalog of trusted applications like Slack, Notepad, Zoom, and more. These rules are kept up to date and can be applied instantly to reduce manual effort. Real-time audit and event-based rules Every MSI and EXE execution is logged and uploaded to the cloud within minutes. Admins can view these events and generate allow/deny rules directly from the UI - closing the loop on what users are running. Integrated privilege management Idemeum’s allowlisting integrates tightly with Endpoint Privilege Management (EPM). A single rule can allow execution and elevate privileges without granting full local admin access - bridging the gap between security and usability. Child process trust inheritance When a trusted app launches a subprocess, trust can be inherited automatically. This prevents legitimate parent-child application chains (e.g., an installer launching a helper binary) from breaking. Application fencing controls Go beyond allowlisting - control what allowed apps can do. Prevent Office apps from launching PowerShell, block browsers from spawning command shells, and isolate potentially risky behaviors. Conclusion Application allowlisting is one of the most powerful defenses against modern threats - but only if it’s implemented in a way that works for both security and operations. idemeum gets it right by combining real-time visibility, flexible policy control, and intelligent defaults. With integrated privilege management, catalog rules, and fine-grained process control, idemeum modernizes allowlisting into a scalable, cloud-native capability fit for the Zero Trust era.

body_text: Shreveport, Louisiana, Jan. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Home Federal Bancorp, Inc. of Louisiana (the “Company”) (Nasdaq: HFBL), the holding company of Home Federal Bank, reported net income for the three months ended December 31, 2025, of $1.675 million compared to net income of $1.020 million reported for the three months ended December 31, 2024. The Company’s basic and diluted earnings per share were $0.55 and $0.54, respectively, for the three months ended December 31, 2025, compared to $0.33 for the three months ended December 31, 2024. The Company reported net income of $3.274 million for the six months ended December 31, 2025, compared to $1.961 million for the six months ended December 31, 2024. The Company’s basic and diluted earnings per share were $1.09 and $1.07, respectively, for the six months ended December 31, 2025, compared to $0.64 for the six months ended December 31, 2024. The Company reported the following highlights during the six months ended December 31, 2025: Book value per share increased to $18.76 at December 31, 2025, from $17.90 at June 30, 2025. Zero dependency on wholesale funding – no brokered deposits or FHLB advances at December 31, 2025 or June 30, 2025. 59 basis point increase to net interest margin compared to the six months ended December 31, 2024. The increase in net income for the three months ended December 31, 2025, as compared to the same period in 2024, resulted from an increase of $777,000, or 16.9%, in net interest income, an increase of $150,000, or 30.7%, in non-interest income, and a decrease of $43,000, or 1.1%, in non-interest expense, partially offset by an increase of $251,000, or 134.2%, in the provision for income taxes, and an increase of $64,000, or 142.2%, in the provision for credit losses. body_text: S ÃO PAULO, Brazil and ATLANTA, Georgia, January 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Descartes Systems Group (Nasdaq:DSGX) (TSX:DSG), the global leader in uniting logistics-intensive businesses in commerce, announced that Supergasbras, one of the leading distributors in the Brazilian liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) market, has modernized its logistics operations using Descartes’ cloud-based route planning and fleet management solution. The solution has helped Supergasbras enhance the efficiency of distribution operations that include over 400 trucks, a team of over 900 people, and the transportation of more than 400,000 tons of LPG per month across Brazil. “This project marks a new stage in our digital transformation and strengthens one of the largest and most complex LPG distribution networks in the country,” said Matteo Lista Netto, National Logistics Intelligence Coordinator at Supergasbras. “Descartes helped us make the route planning process faster, safer and more transparent for everyone involved. The solution’s intuitive interface facilitated adoption by the entire team and, with the use of filters, was easily configured to the characteristics of each region. In addition to more efficient route planning, benefits include fewer stockouts, lower operational costs, and greater reliability in deliveries, especially in regions where demand fluctuates due to seasonality. We’ve also reduced rework caused by communication failures between areas, thanks to the real-time synchronization of route planning information across systems.” Descartes’ route planning and fleet management solution helps distribution-intensive companies in diverse industries plan routes for optimal efficiency, improve delivery performance and minimize the impact of unforeseen events on customer service levels, mileage and costs. With the solution, Supergasbras now automatically plans routes based on up-to-date data using a map-based view of customers as well as real-time visibility of tank levels, consumption rates and customer demand. Delivery management and control tower capabilities provide end-to-end visibility of route execution—from planning to on-site delivery—within a single, integrated environment. The continuous feedback between planning and execution helps companies generate even greater operational gains through data-driven optimization. The Descartes solution also seamlessly integrates with other enterprise systems, including sales and financial applications, replacing previous processes at Supergasbras that relied on the exchange of plain text files to update information across systems. Another significant operational improvement was the integration with Supergasbras’ Faton billing application, which allows drivers to manage all steps of the delivery journey—from route access to invoicing—within a single environment, decreasing errors and administrative workload. “We’re pleased our solution has given Supergasbras a new level of control over its distribution operations,” said Lee Karlinsky, Senior Vice President at Descartes. “The success of this project shows that innovation in logistics goes beyond technology. It’s about collaborating to understand the breadth and depth of Supergasbras’ delivery network and day-to-day operational workflows to drive tangible results for the company and its customers.” Learn more about Descartes’ route execution and fleet performance management solutions and its Routing, Mobile and Telematics solution suite. title: Meet the A-spot: The deep(er) pleasure zone worth knowing about
summary: Learn what the A-spot is, where it’s located, and what research says about pleasure and lubrication (plus, a few tips for exploring).
body_text: The sexual pleasure landscape is full of famous landmarks. The clitoris. The G-spot. The positions everyone swears by. But tucked a little farther in (literally) is a lesser-known area that’s quietly earned a reputation for serious arousal: the A-spot . Short for the anterior fornix erogenous zone (AFE zone), the female A-spot sits deep along the front vaginal wall, closer to the cervix. It doesn’t get nearly as much attention as other pleasure zones, but research and real-world experience suggest it can play a meaningful role in arousal, lubrication, and even orgasm for some people. Let’s break down what the A-spot is, where it lives, and what science (and sex therapists) actually say about it. What is the female A-spot? The A-spot is a sensitive area located on the front wall of the vagina , between the bladder and the cervix. Because it sits deeper than the G-spot, it is sometimes called a “deep spot.” In research papers, this area is referred to as the AFE zone . A well-known study from 1997 looked at what happens when this area is gently and deliberately stimulated. The researchers found that many participants experienced increased natural lubrication and heightened sexual response, even if they had struggled with dryness or discomfort before. 1 Put simply, the A-spot is not a myth . It is a real area of tissue that can respond to stimulation for some people (and, wink, produce fantastic orgasms). Where is the A-spot located? Here’s the easiest way to picture it: It is on the front wall of the vagina , on the same side as the belly It is deeper than the area people usually call the G-spot It is closer to the cervix, which sits at the end of the vaginal canal Because everyone’s body is shaped a little differently, the exact location can vary. That’s one reason some people find it easily and others don’t notice much when exploring. Why the G-spot debate matters here Many guides explain the A-spot by saying something like “find the G-spot, then go a little deeper.” That sounds simple, but there’s an important reason this can be confusing. A large scientific review published in 2021 looked at decades of research on the G-spot and found that scientists do not fully agree on whether it exists as a single, clearly defined structure. Some studies find a sensitive area. Others do not. Location and texture descriptions vary a lot. 2 Interestingly, the review also showed that many people do feel something they describe as a G-spot. In surveys, about six out of ten participants reported having one , even though medical imaging and anatomy studies were inconsistent. 2 This matters because it sets expectations. Internal pleasure areas can be very real in experience, even when science can’t point to one exact spot that looks the same in every body. So, is the A-spot real? Yes, with a caveat. The 1997 AFE-zone study treated the A-spot as a specific stimulation area and measured physical responses. Many participants experienced strong lubrication , and a smaller group experienced orgasm during stimulation. 1 A later case study from 2019 looked at people who experienced expanded sexual responses after exploring less familiar forms of stimulation, including deep vaginal stimulation. The takeaway was not that everyone will respond the same way, but that sexual response can change and broaden for some people over time. 3 Together, these studies support a balanced view. The A-spot exists and can be pleasurable, but it is not a guaranteed button. A-spot vs. G-spot in simple terms Instead of thinking in strict labels, it can help to think in zones. The G-spot is usually described as a sensitive area on the front vaginal wall closer to the opening. The A-spot is described as a sensitive area deeper on that same wall, closer to the cervix. The G-spot review introduces another helpful idea called the clitourethrovaginal complex . This is a way of explaining that pleasure may come from stimulating a group of connected tissues, not one tiny point. 2 That explanation fits well with how many people describe A-spot pleasure, too. What does A-spot stimulation usually feel like? The A-spot doesn’t always feel obvious right away! People often describe it as: A deep pressure rather than a sharp sensation A feeling of fullness or warmth Something that becomes more noticeable as arousal increases One consistent finding in research is lubrication . In the AFE-zone study, increased wetness often showed up early, before peak pleasure. 1 A-spot orgasms and lubrication Some people do experience orgasms linked to A-spot stimulation. In the 1997 study, a portion of participants reported orgasm along with very strong lubrication . 1 These orgasms were often described as deeper or more spread out through the body rather than sharp or localized. That said, orgasm pathways vary widely. The A-spot is one option, not a requirement. Does the A-spot cause squirting? It can play a role, but it’s not that simple. Research suggests that vaginal ejaculation, a.k.a. squirting, is linked to stimulation of the front vaginal wall as a whole , not one single spot. The G-spot review highlights how mixed and inconsistent the evidence is, even after decades of study. 2 A realistic takeaway is that A-spot stimulation might be involved for some people, but it should not be framed as the single cause. Positions that may make A-spot stimulation easier Because the A-spot is deep, positions that allow deeper penetration and front-wall contact tend to work best: Doggy style, especially with a pelvic tilt Cowgirl while leaning back Missionary with hips elevated using a pillow For some, even anal penetration, which can indirectly press against the vaginal wall Comfort and communication are especially important here, since the cervix is nearby. Is A-spot pleasure for everyone? No. Anatomy and sensitivity vary widely. Some people enjoy deep stimulation, while others don’t feel much or find it uncomfortable. Clinical research consistently supports this kind of variation in sexual response. Takeaway: There is no one single correct reaction. A little permission slip before you go Before closing the tab and mentally adding “find the A-spot” to a future to-do list, here is the most important thing to remember: curiosity counts as success . The A-spot does not need to produce fireworks, instant orgasms, or a dramatic personality shift in the bedroom to be worth exploring. Sometimes the win is simply noticing a new sensation . Sometimes it is realizing that deep stimulation is not your thing. Sometimes it is learning that arousal builds more slowly, or differently, than expected. Research helps explain what can happen, but it does not get to decide what should happen. Bodies are not performance-based systems, and pleasure isn’t a scavenger hunt with a prize at the end. So if exploration feels fun, follow that thread. If it feels awkward, boring, or distracting, that is useful information too. The real takeaway is not “everyone should love the A-spot.” It’s that there are more options available than most of us were ever taught, and you get to decide which ones deserve a second date. title: Powering the Future: The Growth of New Energy Storage
summary: Discover how battery energy storage systems (BESS) and smart adhesives enable renewable energy growth. Learn about safety standards, thermal management, and next-gen solutions driving global energy innovation.
body_text: Sustainable energy sources are increasingly meeting energy demands. In the United States, for example, renewable energy use grew by 8.8% from 2024 to 2025 and now generates almost a quarter of the country’s electricity. Further scaling new energy sources, such as solar, wind, and wave power, requires investing in battery energy storage systems (BESS). These units can store energy and discharge electricity as needed, providing a reliable supply for widespread use. Adhesives bond, cool, and insulate BESS components, helping ensure the systems produce power efficiently over their lifespan. In the battery management systems (BMS) that monitor and control battery cell use, adhesives provide similar, critical functions. As BESS design evolves to meet new energy growth, the industry will need innovative adhesive solutions to meet new requirements. The World Needs Smarter, Safer Energy Storage Solutions According to the International Energy Agency, renewable energy sources are on track to meet nearly half of global energy demand by 2030. Global energy storage capacity is expected to reach the terawatt-hour mark in the coming years—a benchmark for describing massive amounts of energy. Energy storage solutions are essential for scaling new energy use because renewable energy sources' production rates can vary. “Solar and wind power are not always ‘on,’” explains Florian Schloegl, Business Manager ePower/Storage and Clean Energy at H.B. Fuller. “Battery energy storage systems can be used to help with supply and demand. Excess energy is stored and then discharged when production is low or when demand increases.” BESS support new energy growth through: Peak shaving: BESS can discharge energy during high periods of demand so that customers do not need to draw from the grid during that time. This reduces the strain on the grid. Grid stabilization: Storing energy in BESS helps ensure electricity is available in times of peak demand. Decentralization: Drawing power from multiple sources decreases a community’s dependence on a single plant. If a local power plant has an emergency shutdown, customers with a grid that also draws from BESS will still have electricity to power essential items, such as medical devices. Optimizing upcoming projects: Large clean energy projects currently in process will require BESS to make the most of all the energy they produce. Inside Today’s Battery Energy Storage Systems A BESS unit typically includes battery modules, a BMS, and an inverter that converts direct current to alternating current to enable the transition of the energy from batteries into the grid or vice versa. All these components are housed in a single structure, typically similar to a storage container. The structure's size, number of batteries, and battery arrangement vary depending on its use. Although BESS designs vary, all systems rely on adhesives and sealants . Adhesives and sealants provide: Structural support and bonding: Adhesives bond BESS components together, such as the cooling plates and battery cells within battery modules. Adhesive manufacturers can formulate adhesives for different levels of structural support, depending on their use. Thermal management: Heat generated by powerful batteries must have somewhere to go. Adhesives and gap fillers pass heat from cells to heatsinks so batteries perform as intended for as long as possible. Encapsulants help prevent thermal runaway, which can lead to fires. If fires do break out in individual cells, encapsulants isolate the cell so the fire doesn’t spread. Protection: Sealants and gaskets protect components from moisture, humidity, and environmental factors that could damage the equipment or decrease its durability. Electrical insulation: Dielectric coatings prevent electricity from arcing between battery components, causing short circuits. Exactly how each sealant or adhesive is used in a BESS depends on the final application. For example, a BESS set on a hard-packed gravel pad in a rural area would not require highly structural adhesives for vibration protection. If this BESS held a large number of extremely dense battery packs that generated substantial heat, however, the batteries would require encapsulant to prevent fires. BESS and BMS: New Energy BFFs Every BESS needs a highly intelligent BMS to monitor battery performance. BMS are electronic systems that track each battery’s state of charge (energy movement in and out of battery cells), record battery capacity, and protect cells from overcharging and overuse. A BMS tracks these metrics throughout each battery's lifetime to determine its state of health, helping operators identify which batteries are ready for replacement. BMS help BESS function better for longer, and the smarter the BMS, the more efficient the BESS. BMS manufacturers rely on adhesives to mount printed circuit board (PCB) components, house PCBs, seal high-voltage connectors and enclosures, and pass heat from PCBs to heatsinks. As BMS become more powerful, they generate more heat, requiring more sophisticated thermal interface materials (TIMs) , such as liquid encapsulants, to spread heat away from the system. Managing New Energy Storage Risks Many BESS systems use lithium-ion batteries, which can overheat during use. Although rare, battery fires can be difficult to extinguish and dangerous. A BMS helps mitigate fire risks by limiting charging to overused cells. In addition, incorporating flame-retardant encapsulants into battery design reduces the risk of a damaging fire. BESS must meet regulatory requirements before use. Common regulations include: UL 9540 – Safety Standard for Energy Storage: Lists criteria for assessing energy storage system hazards, requires communication systems that alert operators of safety issues, and more. UL 9540A – Test Method for Evaluating Thermal Runaway Fire Propagation in Battery Energy Storage Systems: Ensures BESS meet fire safety and building code requirements. NFPA 855 – Standard for the Installation of Stationary Energy Storage Systems: Covers the minimum requirements for mitigating energy storage system risks. Depending on where the BESS is sold, it will likely need to meet additional or different requirements. BESS components undergo testing to ensure they comply with regulations. What’s Next in New Energy Storage Systems Since BESS are not limited by weight or size, they present an exciting opportunity to experiment with emerging materials and battery cell technology. The innovations are endless—and necessary to scale new energy growth. “BESS are quite impressive beasts,” says Michael Cooper, Global Business Development Manager at H.B. Fuller. “There’s a whole different approach to these types of designs and these batteries with many different cell and electrolyte technologies. The technologies pose their own set of problems, but also have their own set of needs.” For years, industry stakeholders have been exploring alternatives to lithium-ion cells. Not only are lithium-ion batteries combustible, but they are expensive to recycle, and extracting lithium is resource-heavy . Other options include sodium-ion cells and solid-state cells. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells present another alternative to lithium-ion cells. Although LFP cells also contain lithium, they have an iron-phosphate cathode rather than the typical nickel, cobalt, and manganese cathode. LFP cell design decreases energy density but improves safety . Since energy density is less critical to BESS design than to other types of electricity storage systems, LFP shows significant promise as a cost-effective, thermally stable, and durable alternative with enhanced discharge and charge efficiency . In addition to adopting new cell technology, BESS can also provide a home for second-life electric vehicle (EV) batteries. These batteries continue to produce energy long after their automotive lifespan has ended. As the number of EVs increases, the number of retired batteries will also increase. Incorporating used EV batteries into BESS rather than disposing of them maximizes their use. In future years, modular BESS systems and AI-driven BMS may become increasingly common. Modular systems provide easier access to cell repair and replacement. Adding modules to BESS to boost capacity is also a cost-effective way to scale compared to remodeling the units. BMS equipped with AI algorithms custom-built to optimize cell use can further extend battery life. How Adhesives Support Next-Generation BESS Advancements in BESS and BMS will require innovative adhesive products. For example, some types of alternative cell technology expand and contract more than lithium-ion cells. Adhesives bonding these cells must be capable of elongating (stretching) without breaking. Although alternative cell technology can reduce fire risks, high temperatures can still prematurely age batteries. Incorporating TIMs into BESS design to remove heat will remain critical to their performance. Adhesive manufacturers can work with customers to either create new products or modify existing formulations. “That’s part and parcel of the solution-oriented approach that we offer to battery manufacturers,” explains Cooper. “We can modify a lot of our materials to facilitate stress management, torsional compression, torque, or even three-dimensional stresses. Having discussions with engineers about what is needed helps us generate and innovate the products that will be used in next-generation applications.” H.B. Fuller Adhesive Solutions for BESS and BMS Adhesives and sealants support new energy storage growth and innovation. H.B. Fuller’s portfolio of BESS and BMS adhesives and sealants includes: EV Protect™ foams mitigate the risk of thermal runaway in BESS units. EV Seal™ sealants, cure-in-place gaskets, and form-in-place gaskets protect battery packs from moisture, dirt, and other environmental hazards. They also provide easy access for maintenance. EV Therm thermally conductive adhesives and gap fillers efficiently dissipate heat to improve battery safety and performance while providing electrical insulation that prevents arcing and improves overall battery efficiency. EV Bond adhesives provide structural support and can replace traditional fasteners, opening up new design possibilities. Driving New Energy Growth, Together Building more efficient BESS units will help new energy producers meet a larger share of domestic and global energy needs. Imagine a wind farm. Beneath the enormous turbines sit a cluster of BESS units, a more humble but invaluable part of new energy production. The future of new energy is here—in the sky, the waves, the wind, and on the ground. When you are ready to discuss adhesive solutions for your BESS challenges , we are here to talk. Let’s work together to drive new energy growth.

title: Most Paywalls Fail Before the User Even Hits Subscribe
summary: Your paywall is not the problem. Everything that happens before it is.
body_text: Your paywall is not the problem. Everything that happens before it is. When apps struggle with conversion, they usually start tweaking the paywall itself — the price, the copy, the button color. But the real issue is almost always upstream. If a user hits your paywall without context, without feeling anything, they are going to bounce. Every time. The problem is sequence, not price Think about what your user has experienced by the time they see a price tag. Did they get a taste of what the app can do? Did they have a moment where they thought, "oh, this is actually useful"? Or did they just see a loading screen and then a paywall? The apps that convert well follow a pattern. First, they give users a sandbox experience where everyone gets the same polished version of the product. The user does something, accomplishes something, feels something. That is the foundation. Make the user sell themselves After the initial experience, smart apps use a short questionnaire. The questions are designed to get users to identify their own problem. When someone types out what they are struggling with, they have done half your sales work for you. They are no longer a cold lead — they are someone who just admitted they need help. Add social proof right before the paywall. Reviews from people who had similar problems. This closes the gap between "I need this" and "I trust this." By the time the paywall shows up, it should feel like the obvious next step. If it feels like a wall, you did not do enough work before it. Stop optimizing the paywall. Start optimizing everything before it.

title: A Practical Guide to Not Lighting Your Sales Budget on Fire With AI
summary: A practical framework to evaluate AI tools, avoid wasted spend, and choose software that delivers real ROI for your business.
body_text: AI tools are everywhere right now. And that’s great…when they’re helpful. But what happens when “ AI ” just becomes shorthand for “dartboard we like to throw money at?” That’s when you start to feel like your business needs more tools, any tools, just to keep up. Enter FOMO: fear of missing out. Rather than slow down and deliberate on an AI strategy, many sales teams just pile tools on top of tools. Soon, AI “solutions” become AI problems: Bloated tech stacks, overlapping subscriptions, nonsensical workflows. And wasn’t AI supposed to simplify our lives ? To prevent these problems, you need a practical framework for being more deliberate about how you choose AI tools. That way, you can avoid overspending on them—and pick up the tools that feel like the perfect fit for your sales team. We’ve got a few ideas to help you along. Start With the Problem, Not the Tool The challenge here is that for many sales teams, AI is a solution in search of a problem . No bueno. What you need is a problem for which an AI tool is designed as a clear solution . Otherwise, you’ll just be fixing what isn’t broken. With AI tools, the strongest use cases tend to involve work that follows a particular set of patterns: Repetitive, time-consuming work, like data entry Work with well-defined inputs and outputs, like lead scoring Tasks that fit into an existing workflow, like automatically assigning leads within a CRM In other words, you need a job to do before you acquire the tool. Don’t invest in the hammers until you’re sure you’ve got a lot of nails to pound in. If AI is so great , why not just throw money at it in hopes it will all work out? Because your ROI will depend on your needs. According to McKinsey , for example, one company with lots of customer service to automate was able to build out 5,000 AI agents. It led to tangible results: AI increased issue resolution by 14% per hour. But what was really enlightening about the company’s experience was the tool-specific improvements: AI helped identify issue resolution during initial contacts much faster AI reduced the overall response time for incoming customers AI also helped customer support increase sales Because so many of its workflows went through customer support, scaling to 5,000 customer service agents made sense. But what about your business? Maybe you’re not worried about 5,000 customers reaching out every week. Look around in your existing workflows. Workflows that depend on software are prime candidates: Lead routing Follow-up email drafting/scheduling Data cleanup Implementing customer research into CRM workflows If it’s a w orkflow that fits inside your CRM , it’s a candidate for AI automation . That makes it a candidate for generating instant ROI when you implement it, preventing frustration and the feeling that you just plopped down a lot of money for a tool with only marginal benefits. What if you don’t have jobs like those ready to go? Hit “pause.” Try to let the feelings of FOMO wash right over you. Because if you don’t, throwing money at AI tools can only introduce more friction and more decisions, eventually adding to the frustration of getting work done. If your workflows are still unclear, the safest move right now is not to buy a tool at all. Get Your House in Order Before You Buy AI Don’t be fooled by the phrase “artificial intelligence.” It’s not yet “artificial wisdom” or “artificial creative thinking.” AI isn’t a catch-all tool just yet , and it’s not going to fix your broken workflows for you. AI systems are essentially algorithms. And they only inherit the quality of the data and the workflows you feed them. If you have messy CRM data or inconsistent workflows, AI might not have clear answers for you. This is the kind of scenario that makes business leaders say: “AI? Tried that. Overrated.” The thing is, it’s not overrated. If you can overcome these challenges and give it clean data and predictable workflows, you’ll be amazed at how quickly it works. You just need clarity in your processes before you automate. Take the company above. They invested in 5,000 AI customer service agents , but they already had systems in place to measure how quickly they were responding to customer queries. Those agents fit into a preexisting customer service workflow. That’s what you need before you invest. Don’t build the skyscraper without digging the foundation first. Match the Job to the Right AI Category Many business leaders evaluate software purchases based on the vendor. “Well, so-and-so has a good reputation. Let’s get a subscription.” That might not be a great approach with AI tools. AI tools make more sense when you evaluate them by category , not because you like a particular vendor. Common categories include: Content generation tools Workflow automation Decision support Data hygiene and analytics Customer interaction Some AI tools fit multiple categories. And your needs are multiple, too. But ideally, you’ll know which category you need most, like a CRM . This will narrow the field of potential tools. And more importantly, it will prevent your team from getting distracted with add-on features that bloat the tech stack without making a meaningful impact. Define ROI Before the Demo You should get a feel for which AI tools are a fit. But you still need one thing: A mindset shift. Ask yourself: how can we hold both ourselves and the tool accountable ? This sets your ROI standards before you opt for a demo or a free trial. To hold the tool accountable for future evaluation, focus on a few variables: Who owns the outcome? Which team is getting assigned the AI tool? Which will use it the most? They’ll have the most critical feedback on how well it performs. When will you review the results? Think about the sample size. If you have 5,000 customer interactions a day, that sample size grows quickly. If you automate a workflow that only triggers once every couple of days, you might need a longer period. How do you measure success? Can you track time saved? Money saved? Or is it simply a “feel” in which you interview your sales reps and ask them if they feel like the AI tool is helping them or not? Set your metrics now, because that will put you ahead of the 66% of companies that struggle to define ROI before they unleash their AI initiatives . (Oh, and by the way: 42% of projects get abandoned due to implementation complexity. Another case for keeping your tools simple.) Whether you define your ROI in terms of revenue gained, costs reduced, time saved, or bottles of Excedrin still full, you need to know whatyou’re trying to accomplish first. When you’re looking at a potential AI tool, you’ll see a lot of buttons: sign up for a demo . So you do. It’s a good idea, too, as you evaluate tools. But remember that these demos are designed to impress you. They don’t address your specific business needs. They don’t frame your ROI for you. They don’t (always) tell you which metrics to watch. You’re the one who has to set these standards in advance. How to Make the Decision Before You Commit to AI Evaluate AI Tools Like You’d Hire a Teammate Buying AI software is less like installing an add-on feature than it is hiring a “digital coworker.” Before you buy, write down three key variables: What the tool “owns” (which process? Which metric?) What the tool isn’t responsible for What success looks like (ROI, revenue generated, time saved, etc.) Like actual hires, your AI's ability to onboard also matters. You don’t want a tool to get you stuck in weeks of setup and fine-tuning. (Just like a hire who takes too long to figure out what you’re doing is potentially a red flag.) And don’t forget to factor in the cost of “babysitting” the tool. Someone on your team will have to implement it, check its outputs, and correct any mistakes . That adds to the time cost, which will affect your ROI if your key variable is “time saved.” Run Small, Time-Boxed Experiments You don’t have to do everything at once. In fact, it’s better if you don’t. AI tools are easiest to evaluate when you give them small, minimalist experiments to pass first. Call it a “pilot program.” Focus on one team or a straightforward workflow, rather than throwing it in the deep end and seeing if the “intelligence” can keep up. Give it two to four weeks. That’s usually enough time to see if your experiment is actually saving time or improving outcomes. But one little tip: do define your criteria for success before you start this test. Prevent Tool Sprawl Before It Starts The simple fact is that the best AI tools reduce the burden on your decision-making. They shouldn’t create more. But “AI tool sprawl” sets in when you throw more and more tools at the many decisions of your workflows. Over time, this sprawl creeps in, and teams thinking “just one more tool” will solve their problems. Then they’re surprised when tools overlap. (Yeah, shocker.) To prevent tool sprawl, give yourself a basic working document to track all of the things you’d like to automate, then assign: What the tool does Which workflow the tool supports Who “owns” the tool internally What it costs The ROI and how you measure it A Simple Framework to Say “No” to Shiny Objects And now, what you’ve been waiting for: permission to say “no” to your FOMO. How can you be sure you’re not missing out? Here’s a framework we like that can help you say no to the shiny objects of AI tools that won’t help you: Remember, cool demos aren’t cool ROI. Not every AI tool deserves a place in your tech stack just because it seems fancy. It’s only worth it if it delivers real results. Bias towards “quiet effectiveness.” We expect AI to be impressive and spectacular. Instead, it works best when it’s just quietly humming and slicing through our old, boring, manual, repetitive tasks. Treat AI as a productivity expander, not a panacea. Evaluate it in terms of improvements , not total fixes. Does it shorten your follow-up time, rather than completely outsource your human emails? Does it automatically assign leads, but still let humans deal with them? Don’t expect it to do everything just yet. Run small experiments . You never know if a tool truly fits until you’re actually hammering in those nails. Choosing the Right AI Tools FOMO exists. There’s no getting around it. But as long as you recognize that FOMO doesn’t need to be satisfied, you’re free to pick smart, quietly practical AI tools that will actually make a difference. We have one for you.
